institution: U.S. Army Center of Military History
text: At the start of the conflict, the Continental Congress created the New York (later, Northern) and Canadian Departments to exercise operational command and control in the areas of active fighting. Congress organized the Middle and Southern Departments in February 1776 as the war spread southward (Map 2). Congress appointed Maj. Gen. Charles Lee to command the Southern Department, which encompassed Virginia, the Carolinas, and Georgia. Lee’s tour of duty was short, but he played an important role in defeating then Maj. Gen. Henry Clinton’s 1776 attack on Charleston. Brig. Gen. Robert Howe of North Carolina took command of the Southern Department when Congress recalled Lee northward in June

1776. Howe lacked an explicit appointment order from Congress, an oversight that allowed state political leaders to challenge Howe’s command authority over state troops. Howe struggled to defend Georgia and South Carolina from raids out of British East Florida. Ultimately, he was recalled after the loss of Savannah and much of Georgia in late 1778.Maj. Gen. Benjamin Lincoln took command of the Southern Department in early 1779. Like Howe, Lincoln experienced significant challenges with civil-military cooperation. His tenure ended with the disastrous loss of Charleston, its garrison, and most of the southern Continental Army in May 1780. Gates took command in July 1780, and soon thereafter led his army to near ruin at Camden in August 1780. Greene thus inherited a command that in two years Map 2

had experienced nothing but defeat; the death or imprisonment of 3,100 Continentals; the loss of Georgia and much of South Carolina; and the loss of thousands of small arms and quantities of cannons, ordnance stores, and other supplies.
citation: Skinner, Harold Allen, Jr. The War in the Carolinas and Georgia, 1781–1782. U.S. Army Campaigns of the Revolutionary War, CMH Pub 71-52. Washington, D.C.: Center of Military History, United States Army, 2026.
title: The War in the Carolinas and Georgia
